sections.h2: Ways to sell a house in Altamonte Springs
sections.html:
An Altamonte Springs owner can list with an agent, sell without one, or take a direct offer from a buyer willing to leave repairs undone. All three finish the same way, with a signed deed, a title search and a recorded transfer in Seminole County.

Altamonte Springs is a Seminole County city with newer apartments and retail around Uptown Altamonte. Even so, the condition of your house, any repairs it needs and whether tenants live there will do more to set your timeline than the street will.

A direct offer may mean a lower price, in return for speed and fewer moving parts. Listing exposes the house to more buyers, though you take on showings, repair requests and the risk of a loan that never funds. Put each offer on paper and compare what you would actually take home after costs.

Selling itself needs no permit, yet half-finished work has a way of turning up when a buyer's inspector visits. Permits run through the city's Building and Fire Safety Department and Civic Access, its online portal.

Contractors use the portal for permits without plan review, for status checks and for booking inspections. Jobs that need plan review go in on paper, by mail, or on a USB flash drive the city keeps. A homeowner pulling a permit has to come in person. If you did work yourself, ask the department whether a permit applied and whether it was closed out.

City departments for permit and business questions

Permits and inspectionsBuilding and Fire Safety(407) 571-8433

If you rented the house out before selling, ask the City Clerk whether a business tax receipt applies.

The county, not the city, values your parcel and mails the bill, with the city among several taxing bodies. Each August, the county appraiser's TRIM notice shows taxable value, proposed millage and budget meeting dates.

Setting rates isn't the appraiser's job, and the collector mails final bills by November 1. Pay in November for a 4 percent discount, with the reward shrinking to 1 percent by February. Anything unpaid on April 1 is delinquent. For questions about value, classification or exemptions, call the appraiser at 407-665-7506.

To dispute value, petition the county's Value Adjustment Board, which the county clerk runs, no later than 25 days after the notice is mailed. A buyer's first bill often runs higher than a long-time owner's, because a sale resets homestead value.

sections.h2: Florida transfer taxes and recording costs
sections.html:
The biggest transfer cost in Florida is deed stamp tax, at 70 cents per $100 of consideration. The clerk collects it at recording. Each party to the deed stays answerable to the state, whatever the contract says.

The contract assigns the payer. A mortgage on the property counts as consideration even when the buyer doesn't take it over. Recording charges follow state law and the clerk's own schedule, so ask the Seminole County clerk for current figures.

  • Documentary stamp tax on the deed.
  • The clerk's recording fee.
  • Back taxes and liens, settled from your proceeds.
  • A payoff of each mortgage of record.

Our Florida property tax guide explains discounts and caps.

sections.h2: Recording the deed in Seminole County
sections.html:
Your deed is filed with the Seminole County Clerk of Court, who records it and takes in the stamp tax. The appraiser then updates ownership, and the next TRIM notice goes to the new owner.

Before closing, the title agent should find any mortgage, lien or judgment filed against you. Ask for a written payoff list and the clerk's current fee schedule, since the county sets its own recording charges.

With tenants in the house, list their deposits and prepaid rent in the closing paperwork.

A foreclosure and an estate each have their own timetable, and either can still end in a sale. Once a Florida court enters a foreclosure judgment, the clerk holds the public sale 20 to 35 days out, unless the plaintiff agrees to wait.

The top bidder puts 5 percent down. With no objection inside 10 days, the clerk issues the certificate of title. Any surplus is claimed through the clerk. A sale you make before that date puts the price in your hands.

For an inherited house, a simpler summary administration is available when the estate is $150,000 or less, or when the owner died more than two years ago. No Florida estate tax applies to deaths after 2004, and a personal representative's deed under a probated will carries no deed stamps.

A lease may continue after the sale. An investor buyer won't mind, but someone who wants to move in will. A month-to-month tenancy ends on 30 days' notice, while a year-to-year one needs 60.

Unpaid rent brings a 3-day written notice that doesn't count weekends or court holidays. Other lease breaches carry a 7-day notice. Once a judgment is entered, the sheriff carries out a writ after posting 24 hours' notice.

Read the lease before you promise a closing date, and disclose it early to any buyer.

Gather the signed lease, the deposit amount and the rent ledger, and give copies to the title agent. If the tenant plans to stay, ask the buyer for that in writing. If the tenant must leave, put the move-out date in the contract so no one is surprised at closing.

sections.h2: City services that change hands with the house
sections.html:
The city's home page links to services you'll want to move or stop.

  • Trash and recycling, to set up or end service when ownership changes.
  • Online payments, for city bills and fees.
  • Permits, through the Civic Access portal.
  • Agendas and minutes, if a zoning or code item affects your street.
  • A disaster resource guide, useful for buyers moving from out of state.

County offices still handle tax and recording. Those pages answer the everyday questions that arise before you hand over keys.

Whatever route you pick, a few habits keep the sale tidy. Start by pulling together your deed, latest mortgage statement and any permit records. Ask your title agent exactly which papers they need from you, and by what date. Ask for every offer in writing, then compare the amount you'd net once taxes, recording fees and payoffs come out, not the headline price.

Before signing, read the contract for who pays each closing cost, the closing date, and what happens if an inspection finds problems. A direct cash purchase skips lender appraisals and many financing delays, yet the title search, deed recording and tax settlement still happen.

Confirm where the proceeds will go and how you'll receive them, and ask when you must hand over keys and remove belongings. Cancel utility service only after closing is confirmed. Hold on to copies of everything you sign, plus the final settlement statement.

faqs.q: What is my Altamonte Springs home worth?
faqs.a: No reliable number can be given without looking at your house. Get written offers or an appraisal, and compare what each leaves you after costs.

faqs.q: Who sets property tax in Altamonte Springs?
faqs.a: Seminole County values and bills the parcel, and the city is one taxing authority. The appraiser does not set rates.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to sell my house?
faqs.a: Not just to sell. Unfinished permitted work can still surface in an inspection, so call Building and Fire Safety at (407) 571-8433.

faqs.q: What is the Florida deed stamp tax?
faqs.a: It's 70 cents per $100 of consideration. The contract names the payer, but the law reaches every party.

faqs.q: Can I sell with a tenant in the house?
faqs.a: Yes. The lease usually continues, and a month-to-month tenancy ends only with 30 days' notice.
